item.title: Lutnick under fire over ties to Jensen Huang and Nvidia's China chip exports
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, left, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, right speak in the Cross Hall of the White House before an event on "Investing in America" on April 30, 2025. Trump was joined by CEOs to highlight companies and their investments in the United States during the event. - Andrew Harnik/Getty Images The first call, as Jensen Huang remembers it, came from Howard Lutnick. It was around the start of Donald Trump’s second term, and Lutnick was preparing to become his Commerce Secretary. His message to the head of Nvidia was simple: whenever you need the president, call us. Recounting the call on Joe Rogan’s podcast last December, Huang remembered fondly that Lutnick had called him and his company “a national treasure.” Two years later, Huang has resigned from Nvidia and Lutnick is under intense scrutiny for what some Trump advisers see as inaction in placing limits on US chip exports to China and his role in cultivating Huang as a top administration ally. Other administration officials have accused Lutnick of bucking internal consensus and Trump’s own directives in failing to blacklist an Nvidia customer suspected of funneling chips to China. Some of Trump’s advisers, reeling from the fallout of Huang’s resignation, have begun discussing whether Lutnick should be dismissed, according to people familiar with the conversations. This account is derived from more than a dozen sources, including officials inside the administration and the tech industry. They described a rapidly deepening relationship that came to influence nearly all areas of the White House’s stance toward some of the most powerful technology in the world. Questions surrounding the scandal — and the fresh push to limit sales of advanced chips to China — are likely to persist as Trump prepares to meet next week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, the hub of China’s tech industry. American officials said they didn’t expect Trump to raise the alleged spying with Xi, and said China wouldn’t have a say in whether Washington tightens restrictions on access to chips. ‘What the hell is Nvidia?’ Until shortly after Trump’s inauguration last year, Huang was nearly a stranger to Trump’s world. He would skip the swearing-in to spend Lunar New Year with employees in Asia, while his tech titan counterparts Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos had prime spots in the Capitol Rotunda. Trump, by his own account, had barely heard of Nvidia or its CEO: “What’s his name? What the hell is Nvidia?” he recalled wondering a few months later. “I’ve never heard of it before.” His ignorance wouldn’t last long. Eleven days after being sworn in for a second term, Trump met Huang at the White House. Huang also met that day with Lutnick, still awaiting confirmation as Commerce Secretary. As Trump signed executive orders in the Oval Office later that afternoon with the cameras rolling, he was full of praise for the man he’d only recently met. “He’s a great gentleman, and I hadn’t met him,” Trump said as he reflected on what he called a good meeting. “He’s the biggest in the world in terms of chips.” Over the next two years, the relationship would deepen over dinners, phone calls and many, many meetings. It was aided at every step by Lutnick, who helped elevate Huang’s profile and whose agency is responsible for keeping sensitive American technology away from adversaries. unknown content item - On Thursday, after Huang resigned from Nvidia following revelations he had extramarital affairs with two women, one of whom may be connected to China , Lutnick’s critics began circling. Administration officials who have long been concerned about Huang’s influence on Trump said privately that the Commerce Department failed to crack down on chip shipments to companies suspected of passing them on secretly to China. Speaking on CNBC Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a wide swath of Trump’s administration — including the Treasury and State departments, the Pentagon and the US Trade Representative — favored placing the company at the center of the scandal, Megaspeed, on an export blacklist. He said it was the Commerce Department, led by Lutnick, that had failed to follow through. “Commerce…has the pen…and you will have to ask them about their internal process,” he said. Both Republicans and Democrats on Capitol Hill demanded Lutnick answer questions about what he knew, and when. House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrats wrote to Lutnick demanding to know what he and his export control chief, Jeffrey Kessler, knew about Megaspeed, and when. Senate Democrats directed Lutnick to preserve documents, communications and records related to Nvidia’s exports of advanced chips. “This news is as concerning as it gets,” Sen. Jim Banks, a Trump ally, said Thursday on Fox News. “When you’re in a war with another country, you don’t give them your best technologies. And that’s why lawmakers, for the last two years, have been pushing hard to stop our high-end computer chips from being exported to China.” The White House said Thursday Trump “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history.” A deepening relationship A few months after Huang’s first Oval Office meeting, Lutnick played a role in facilitating Huang’s attendance at a $1-million-a-head MAGA Inc. dinner at Mar-a-Lago, according to two people familiar with the matter. The April dinner proved fateful. Huang used it to make a final appeal against planned restrictions on selling Nvidia’s H20 chip to Chinese customers. Trump, meanwhile, walked away impressed with his new, extraordinarily wealthy friend. Huang’s charm offensive at the Palm Beach dinner seemed to work, but only briefly. The White House moved to shelve the planned curbs. But as a trade war with China heated up, Nvidia later disclosed that the government had told it that H20 sales to China would require a license – and that the requirement would stay in place indefinitely. Huang kept working at it. At an Investing in America event at the end of April 2025, Lutnick and Huang were photographed together in the Cross Hall. Trump turned the moment into a show of affection. “I could have Jensen negotiating. He’d blow my people away,” Trump said. “Even Howard would say that.” Lutnick, sitting in the audience, quickly concurred. “We’ll take him.” By July, Huang was back in the Oval Office. His pitch this time was tailored to Trump. Selling chips to China, he argued, could create American jobs and cement American AI as the world standard. He had already said publicly in May that the ban already cost Nvidia $15 billion in sales. Jensen Huang, then CEO of Nvidia, center, speaks with Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin during the "Winning the AI Race" summit at the Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium in Washington, DC, on July 23, 2025. Trump signed executive orders related to his Artificial Intelligence Action Plan during the event. - Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images Two top administration officials who had become close Huang allies accompanied him in the Oval Office: Lutnick and David Sacks, the White House AI adviser, who championed “exporting the US AI stack” – the idea that selling older chips like the H20 abroad keeps the world hooked on American technology. Five days later, Nvidia announced the government had assured it that it would be permitted to sell the H20 in China. Huang was in Beijing when he said sales would resume. The next day, Lutnick went on CNBC, explaining the decision as a way to get China “addicted to the American technology stack.” The H20 deal was finished in August, and the president negotiated it himself, directly with Huang, as they sat face-to-face in the White House. Lutnick’s agency immediately moved to issue H20 licenses. Trump would go on to publicly confirm the arrangement that made the H20 sales possible: Nvidia would pay the government 15% of its China chip revenue. Through the fall, Huang drew closer to the president, and Trump regularly mentioned Huang off-the-cuff in his public remarks. In October, Trump spoke with Huang, Marc Benioff and other business leaders about sending federal law enforcement into San Francisco, and the next day he called the plan off, citing those conversations. That same month, as Trump was preparing to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in South Korea, Nvidia donated $25 million to Trump’s White House ballroom project, a person familiar with the matter said. Nvidia never appeared on the published donor list. The warnings In the summer of 2025, as Trump and Huang were growing closer, a phone call began to unravel something larger. Singapore police, investigating a cloud company called Megaspeed, questioned its former managing director, Alice Huang, and barred her from leaving the country. She had met Jensen Huang at an Nvidia event in California in early 2024. The two were photographed together at a trade show in Taipei that June. During a briefing with lawmakers on Capitol Hill at the end of 2025, federal agents said they suspected Jensen Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort,” citing his close relationship with Alice Huang, according to sources familiar with the meeting. Jensen Huang, then CEO of Nvidia, with a woman confirmed by a Reuters source to be Alice Huang in Taipei, Taiwan released on June 7, 2024. - Obtained by Reuters The briefing was centered on an investigation into suspected efforts to circumvent US export control restrictions and attempts to influence the Trump administration’s policy on shipping certain Nvidia chips to China, according to the sources. The FBI, which is conducting the primary counterintelligence investigation, told lawmakers last year that it was particularly suspicious of Alice Huang’s seemingly overnight career pivot from Chinese State television journalist to businesswoman with an unusually large amount of purchasing power in the Chinese economy, one of the sources said. Trump himself had been briefed on intelligence about Alice Huang in late 2025 and took no action, CNN previously reported. But the investigations continued. The Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 to determine whether the firm had run afoul of US export rules, but had stopped short of placing the company on the so-called Entity List, a trade blacklist that bars US suppliers from selling to listed firms without a license. Other areas of the administration had grown frustrated at the delay, including at the State Department and National Security Council, people familiar with the matter said. On Capitol Hill, Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Tom Cotton, an Arkansas Republican, had taken notice and quickly fired off a direct request to Lutnick to investigate Megaspeed. Behind the scenes, executive branch officials from other national security agencies were raising Megaspeed as a clear target for investigation and inclusion on Commerce’s Entity List. The logo of data center company Megaspeed International at its office in Singapore on November 10. - Taryn Ng/AFP/Getty Images They got no substantive response. And in meetings when the case came up, Lutnick’s deputies would respond by telling officials little more than it was Lutnick’s decision to make, according to people familiar with the conversations. In the CNBC interview Friday, Bessent suggested the inaction had violated directives given by Trump himself. “I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s,” Bessent said, referring to an older-generation data-center chip. “And so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, gives the Chinese an advantage.” When Trump was preparing to travel to China for a state visit in May, the delegation announced on May 11 initially didn’t include Huang. The next day, Trump phoned Huang to invite him. As Trump flew aboard Air Force One to Anchorage that afternoon with Elon Musk and Sean Hannity, he received a briefing from Secretary of State Marco Rubio about some of the concerns surrounding Huang and China. On the ground in Alaska, Huang boarded for the final leg to Beijing. On May 14, Xi greeted Trump at the Great Hall of the People, and Musk, Huang and Apple’s Tim Cook were the only executives the White House listed at the arrival ceremony. Huang called it “one of the most important summits in human history.” Members of the Trump administration are joined by Jensen Huang, second row right, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, centre right in the second row, and Apple CEO Tim Cook, center left middle row, at a welcome ceremony for President Donald Trump at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing on May 14. - Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images In the months that followed, there was little to indicate Trump or Lutnick had concerns about Huang. Trump praised him in the Oval Office. Lutnick, moderating a September G20 session in North Carolina, called him “an American treasure” — the same flattery deployed on their first phone call nearly two years earlier. In September, Huang took a call from Trump on stage and put him on speakerphone at a summit in Los Angeles. Trump called AI-takeover fears “a hoax,” called data centers “the oil of the next 20, 25 years,” and said opposition played into China’s hands. Ten days later, Huang and his wife were at the White House to attend Trump’s State Dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping. They were seated at the head table with the two leaders and their spouses. The reckoning Less than a month later, the first bombshell dropped: US officials had concluded Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset who had cultivated a close relationship with Jensen Huang. CNN later reported the US intelligence community is still working to understand the relationship between Alice Huang and the Chinese government, with multiple sources telling CNN that the intelligence collected on her to date does not prove that she was acting as a spy for Beijing. Trump, officials said, would not hang his friend out to dry. As one official put it, Huang’s problems were Nvidia’s, Nvidia’s were the economy’s, and that became the president’s problem. Trump called Huang “brilliant” and, “unless we find out something to the contrary,” “very above board.” President Donald Trump takes questions with AI executives after a meeting on artificial intelligence outside the West Wing of the White House on September 29. - Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images But the political ground had also shifted. Democrats won both chambers in the midterm elections, and voters rejected data-center projects in 40 of 41 ballot measures. The Republican chairs of three House committees – Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and the China select committee, all set to lose their gavels in January – asked Huang as well as Nvidia’s general counsel for closed-door interviews next month. Kessler, Lutnick’s deputy at the Commerce Department, has also been asked to appear at a hearing scheduled for next month. Republicans are now accusing Lutnick of putting Trump in a vulnerable position. “Shame on Lutnick for allowing that exposure to happen for the president. Raises a question about what other ones are out there,” Sen. Thom Tillis told reporters Thursday. During a meeting in the Situation Room last week, Treasury Secretary Bessent turned to Lutnick and asked why Megaspeed wasn’t on the entities list. According to sources familiar with the meeting, Lutnick stammered, “I don’t know. I’ll look into it.” For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/15/politics/lutnick-jensen-alice-huang-trump-nvidia

item.title: FAA was warned for years about repair risks leading to nationwide ground stop
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Federal aviation officials were repeatedly warned that the push to rapidly modernize the nation's air traffic control system risked breaking it, with the potential dangers spelled out in government reports in the months and years leading up to Friday's nationwide ground stop that halted flights for nearly 4½ hours coast to coast. A government watchdog report in September cautioned that the way the old, legacy systems were being replaced could result in disruptions - including ground stops. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. A separate Federal Aviation Administration-commissioned safety review in 2023 also warned about potential air traffic disruptions from the agency's technology updates, saying the FAA needed to ensure the old systems were preserved during the critical changeover period. The predicted disruptions arrived Friday, resulting in more than 12,000 flight cancellations with outrage and delays rippling across the weekend. Federal officials blamed a remote, overloaded router that a contractor was installing as part of a long-running effort to replace copper wires with fiber cables for air traffic communications nationwide. The router was sending "over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds," causing "instability" with the system that allows controllers to talk with planes cruising at high altitudes, Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy said Saturday. Duffy painted it as an isolated incident, saying it was either a contractor's error or faulty equipment. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said they needed to push ahead with the work. "It will continue to break until we replace it," he said. But the September report from the Government Accountability Office found that the FAA's approach to delivering Duffy's so-called Brand New Air Traffic Control System has prioritized "speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and potential disruptions." The effort involves more than 11,000 individual projects that GAO found were not being run with an overarching schedule. Individual facilities could have upgrades spread across multiple visits, GAO said, "without addressing potential conflicts, optimizing the schedules, or reducing disruptions to air traffic control operations." "Their approach could be a sound approach," said an FAA technical official, speaking on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the project publicly. "The problem is it hasn't been fleshed out." The official said the FAA's approach carries risks because it involves making changes to a fragile, always-on system. "Think about a car," the official said. "I'm not just going to throw a new engine in there while it's moving." In response to a question about why the work was carried out on a flight-heavy Friday afternoon, Duffy cited the urgency of the upgrades, which he said were being carried out in a remote location far from major flight corridors. But, he said, "there will be a reevaluation of when we do this work." The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union released a statement Saturday saying: "Historically, contractors have followed a protocol where FAA employees conduct a risk assessment and coordinate the maintenance of the system or equipment. PASS-represented technicians were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop yesterday." The FAA and the Transportation Department did not respond to requests for comment about the government reports warning of the risks of modernization efforts. Aviation experts and federal officials agree on the need to update the aging technology behind the nation's air traffic control systems. Efforts have been discussed for years, but action has been fitful. Duffy made modernization a top agency goal when he took over under President Donald Trump last year. Duffy has often touted the speed of the agency's progress, while decrying the floppy disks, paper strips and antiquated computer parts still needed for controllers to safely guide planes through the nation's airspace. One air traffic controller, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak with the media, confirmed that their co-workers sometimes need to source parts on eBay because the original manufacturer no longer makes it. That was the case with a recent piece needed for one control tower's ground radar system. "It was a two-week wait while we waited for the part to be delivered after it was ordered on eBay," the controller said. Last year, Duffy asked Congress for $31.5 billion to fund the Brand New Air Traffic Control System. He got $12.5 billion last summer to start. Duffy said Saturday he wants to do far more than just replace copper wires with fiber cables. Among the items on his wish list: updating many of the nation's aging flight control towers. The copper-to-fiber switch appeared to pick up speed last year under a federal contractor, L3Harris Technologies. Now, an estimated 70 percent of the work had been completed, Duffy said. The U.S. firm is a major defense contractor and tech services provider that also happens to own the wired network serving, for the moment, as the air traffic control system's nervous system. Duffy, however, pointed the finger at L3Harris repeatedly on Saturday for the problems that led to the ground stop. "We're going to hold people accountable," he said, adding: "Many of our contractors take our money and provide really poor service to us. Full stop." An L3Harris spokesman said it was supporting the FAA's investigation "to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel." It was unclear following Saturday's news conference with federal transportation officials why a single problematic router caused chaos across the country. Tom Lintner, a former safety official at the FAA, said a disruption like Friday's could recur if changes are not made. "There's a risk of this happening again, if they still try to push this modernization, which is necessary, on an unrealistic time frame," Lintner said. Lintner said he wanted to know whether the FAA conducted a safety case for the project, which would outline what could go wrong, the risks and how to mitigate them. "They installed the receiver and it overpowered the system. That has a logical ring to me," Lintner said. "The comeback question is: So you didn't see this coming? And does that mean you experimented in trying to push this through because you've got this deadline at the next inauguration that you've got to get this done?" "This has shades of the ballroom and arch," he said, referring to other legacy-oriented projects by the Trump administration. In November 2023, a group of aviation experts delivered a report on the safety of the nation's airspace. The report noted that the copper-wired communications backbone among facilities used technology so old that it is "no longer supported by the telephone companies' lines on which the signals are actually carried." The FAA had continued to use the ancient system for budgetary reasons, and the agency knew it needed to move on. In July 2023, the FAA identified the Federal Telecommunications Infrastructure as among the highest-level risks to airspace safety. But the experts' report noted that moving to the proposed solution, set to take more than a decade to build out, also carried "the risk of losing communication with the rest of the (national air space) due to an unplanned failure." On Friday, that's what happened. A former senior official familiar with the experts' report said there had been plans for the experts to examine other safety issues with the nation's air traffic control system. The FAA under President Joe Biden commissioned the group to launch a new inquiry in October 2024. The group's first new meeting came shortly before Trump was inaugurated in January 2025. But weeks after Trump took office, with new FAA officials in control, the group learned it was being disbanded. No one seemed interested any longer in what they might discover, the former official said. Vincent van Gogh's Châtaigniers en fleurs is displayed ahead of this week's auction [Reuters] Auction house Sotheby's says it is working to resolve a dispute over the intended sale of a painting by Vincent van Gogh. Châtaigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom"), which carries an estimated value of $180m (£136m), is due to go under the hammer in New York on Wednesday. But representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - say it may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis. Sotheby's says its own "extensive research" has not established this, but that it will work with the family to try and reach a solution. "Sotheby's takes provenance and restitution matters extremely seriously and has undertaken extensive research into the ownership history of Châtaigniers en fleurs," the auction house told the BBC in a statement. "We are aware of the concerns recently raised by representatives of the Fischer heirs and have been in dialogue with them regarding the painting's history. "While our research to date has not established that the painting was sold under duress, we recognise the importance of engaging thoughtfully and constructively with the family and are committed to working toward a mutually satisfactory resolution." The painting is being sold as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection. Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890. It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934. The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotherby's says. Four other owners have had it prior to it being put up for auction this year. Fischer family heirs have instructed a lawyer who, according to the New York Times , has written to Sotherby's on their behalf. He is said to have told the auction house the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. item.title: Biggest waves in a decade pound California beaches and flood streets
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Chris Aceves, center, with the help of friends Natalie Nunez and David Lechuga, carries a sandbag to protect his Pacifica home from flooding caused by huge waves Saturday. From left: Natalie Nunez, Chris Aceves and David Lechuga try to protect Aceves' home from flooding caused by huge waves Saturdasy in Pacifica. (Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle) The Bay Area's biggest waves in more than a decade slammed the California coast Saturday, flooding streets, endangering homes and threatening to engulf anyone who got too close. The waves attracted onlookers from the North Bay to Santa Cruz County, dousing many with cold water as they ran to higher ground. Related: California could see another round of mammoth waves within days Pacifica was hit especially hard, with large waves consistently crashing over its seawall and flooding city streets. Every 30 minutes or so, a wave that appeared to be double the size of the previous one pushed water hundreds of feet inland. Onlookers were soaked by the towers of water, sometimes knocking people off their feet and sending them scrambling in many directions. Rocks, kelp and other debris surrounded the famous Taco Bell Cantina, and nearly a foot of floodwater along Highway 1 prevented cars from entering the parking lot. A high surf warning was in effect until Sunday morning for "life-threatening" waves of 25 to 35 feet, potentially 50 to 60 feet at steep shorelines such as Mavericks in Half Moon Bay, the National Weather Service said. As of 9 a.m. Saturday, significant wave heights - the average of the highest third of waves - were measured up to 31 feet at a buoy offshore Point Reyes, the second largest in three decades of records. Only in December 2015 were waves bigger, by less than a foot. Maximum waves are often 1.8 times bigger than the significant wave height. Waves probably surpassed 50 feet at many offshore buoys, though there are limited official measurements along the immediate coast. "Typically, the largest waves arrive in December and January, and only one time in the 27-year record of the Point Reyes buoy have forecast wave heights been this large in November," the Scripps Institution of Oceanography said in a social media post. Homeowners and renters scramble as massive waves flood garages, basements and cars in Pacifica during one of California's largest wave events in decades. 🎥: Anthony Edwards Read more >> https://t.co/p4lpCNWRE2 https://t.co/0kcbjLv0Vd - San Francisco Chronicle (@sfchronicle) November 14, 2026 Another large swell was expected late Sunday into Monday, with rough seas continuing through the week as more storms spin off the California coast. Erin Shea, a renter at the end of Elder Lane in Pacifica, said floodwater damaged personal belongings in her garage. Adam Drake watches as flooding from high waves inundates a street outside his Pacifica home Saturday. (Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle) Adam Drake, a beachfront homeowner farther up Elder Lane, said the scenes of the waves were "unprecedented," with only 2023 bringing more furious flooding. Recently installed pumps were not working to drain floodwater at the end of the road. Marc Ramos, who surfs at Rockaway Beach in Pacifica at least twice a week, said Saturday's rip currents arrived early in the season and made surfing impossible. "This is just the beginning of the surf season," Ramos said as he checked out the scene. "I've seen it like this, but in mid-January. This is kind of odd. We haven't even hit Thanksgiving yet." Ramos said anyone getting too close to the waves could be swept out to sea pretty quickly. "Don't go out," he said. "Definitely don't go out." Near the Pacifica Pier, a constant stream of onlookers flocked to the waterfront on foot despite closures on adjacent streets due to safety concerns. Several spectators, including a mother carrying a toddler, were caught in a sneaker wave and knocked down in the parking lot in front of the Pacifica City Council Chambers. The mother and toddler were able to get up with the help of bystanders who immediately jumped in to assist. About 50 people stood along San Francisco's Ocean Beach near Sunset Dunes park watching the waves late Saturday morning. The tide went all the way to the dune in front of the parking lot. Among the onlookers was Emir Molina, who has been fishing on Ocean Beach since he moved to San Francisco 26 years ago. The waves were far too big for him to fish Saturday, he said. Molina said the waves were the biggest he's seen in all those years. November is later than he usually sees vicious waves along the coast of San Francisco, he said. They usually come in October, and they don't go nearly as far out. "I have a ton of respect for the ocean," he said. "A ton of respect." Waves crash onto the Pacifica coast Saturday. (Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle) In Marin County, Richard Delameter came to Point Reyes Beach from Novato to watch the waves. "Why am I here? Because nature, when she is furious, is completely dramatic. I like the drama of watching the earth when she's angry," he said. Delameter said he had been coming to Point Reyes since 1967. Earlier Saturday, he was picking up debris from the beach "but the ranger told me to get my ass up to higher ground." With high tide coming at 12:45 p.m., Delameter said "another hour and I can get back to college football." Onlookers check out the waves Saturday at Point Reyes Beach. (J.K. Dineen/S.F. Chronicle) While the waves were dramatic, U.S. Park Service volunteer Susan Aaron said the sunshine and relatively light breeze were having a moderating effect. "If the wind was blowing another 20 miles per hour, the waves would be right up to the base of the dunes," she said. Aaron said she is expecting the winter to bring extensive damage to the California coast. "The coastal communities are in real trouble. People are unaware of the power of nature." Redwood City resident Edward Dorville went to Stinson Beach, but the surf there was not too impressive so he drove to Point Reyes. "Here the surf is more irregular so I thought there would be more impact. Humbling is the word," he said. "It's a reminder." Workers watch tidal water in Soquel Creek during high surf Saturday in Capitola (Santa Cruz County). (Noah Berger/For the S.F. Chronicle) The Santa Cruz County Sheriff's Office issued a weekend evacuation warning for low-lying coastal areas due to significant wave activity and hazardous surf conditions. "Large waves have the potential to reach coastal homes and properties, causing dangerous flooding and making access to affected areas difficult or unsafe," the sheriff's office said. The National Weather Service warned spectators to keep a safe distance from the waves all along the California coast. Onlookers scramble as a wave breaks at Steamer Lane in Santa Cruz on Saturday. (Noah Berger/For the S.F. Chronicle) "Dangerously large breaking waves can overpower swimmers, pulling people into the sea from beaches, jetties, and rocks resulting in significant physical injury and increasing the risk of drowning," the weather service said. "Waves can sweep across the shoreline without warning." Huge waves are a hallmark of El Niño , and experts say repeated rounds of waves this winter could cause billions of dollars in damage along the California coast, especially if they hit during high tides. "El Niño-driven changes in tropical weather patterns are shifting storm paths across the North Pacific, bringing stronger storms and bigger waves to the California coast," Scripps said in its social media post. "During El Niño, storms also tend to track farther south, forming closer to California and increasing wave activity along the coast." Waves break at the Walton Lighthouse in Santa Cruz on Saturday. (Noah Berger/For the S.F. Chronicle) These large waves generate tremendous energy. The relationship between wave heights and energy is a squared relation, meaning a 40-foot wave slams into the coast with four times as much energy as a 20-foot wave. Along the California coast, wave power is 32% stronger during strong El Niños than a typical year. Wave-producing storms are becoming larger with climate change, and rising sea levels are contributing to more coastal damage, previous research found. item.title: Judge temporarily blocks Trump from moving ahead on golf course redevelopment
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge on Saturday ordered a two-week delay to any work at a historic Washington public golf course not far from the White House, blocking for now President Donald Trump's push to redevelop the site along the Potomac River into a championship-level venue. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the temporary restraining order before the East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months. Trump had announced work would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers . The plaintiffs argue that Trump's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something the Republican president denies. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would “irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest." The president's public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the decision. Trump said on Oct. 26 that “We are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th in order to renovate and rebuild for Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons.” He added that the goal was to renovate and rebuild ”a World Championship Public Facility." Reyes in her ruling Saturday noted that Trump's posts presented a problem for the government. “They indicate that the Washington National Plan is final and that NPS will close the Park to implement it,” she wrote. “Both points favor granting Plaintiffs’ motion for another temporary restraining order.” Reyes said her order “ENJOINS the government from closing East Potomac Park and the East Potomac Golf Course during the daily hours in which they were open as of November 14, 2026. It does not order the Government to undertake any active management of either. Further, for the avoidance of any doubt, the Government remains free, as it has since the onset of this litigation, to conduct repairs on any part of the Park and Course with any notice required by the existing Preliminary Injunction.” The judge said the order is in effect “through November 28, 2026, or further order from the Court, whichever comes first.” The Justice Department said in a statement Saturday that the judge acknowledged that the National Park Service can limit access to its facilities where the public is at risk of harm. “Nothing in the Court’s order precludes planning for the development of a world class golf course to continue,” it said. "The Department of Justice will always vociferously defend the Trump Administration’s agenda in court.” Catherine Carroll, a senior legal adviser at Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs, praised the ruling. “We are grateful that once again, a court has intervened to prevent irreparable harm caused by the Trump-Vance administration’s pursuit of another one of the president’s vanity projects,” she said. “The administration’s inexplicable drive to destroy East Potomac Park would have taken away a treasured park that could never be replaced." The park’s redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch , a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts , among others. Reyes had signaled throughout a five-hour court hearing Friday that she was likely to issue some stoppage for the park closure. The only issue was how expansive it might be. Justice Department lawyer Adam Gustafson argued that the entire East Potomac Park, which includes three golf courses, a miniature course, bike riding lanes and other recreational areas, was being closed because of safety factors. He also noted that the lease between the government and the current operator, National Links Trust, was ending Sunday. Reyes pointed out that safety had not been part of the discussion over the closure for months and that ending the lease felt more like an action that provided a premise for the closure rather than an action that led to the closure of the course about 2 miles from the White House. Even before the order, Trump lashed out in a social media post Saturday, contending that Reyes “doesn’t want us to quickly and inexpensively fix up the Course which is, also, very dangerous.” He said people who live in the Washington area would get a 50% discount on “any and all Rates charged” and that the redevelopment would “evolve into something very special, something which the Judge will be able to take great pride in seeing!” Reyes’ order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump’s projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch , a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project. Reyes, who was nominated to the court by Democratic President Joe Biden, had for months been reticent about approving the plaintiffs’ requests for work stoppages. The plaintiffs had argued the administration was moving ahead with work related to the project despite the pending lawsuit. Her reluctance to issue orders ended in October, spurred in part by a tree-cutting spree by the administration over a holiday weekend with little notification to the judge or plaintiffs. Officials and government lawyers said the tree work was part of a 2019 plan that recommended the cutting. In response, the judge confronted the administration over what she portrayed as deceitful actions over its intentions for the project. Reyes has repeatedly expressed frustration over the minute planning details she has been asked to adjudicate, including over the trees being cut down at the 106-year-old park. The Justice Department filed a request that Reyes be removed from the case because of what it called her “egregious behavior” and questioned her impartiality. Reyes has not recused herself. The restraining order was one of two issues Reyes took up during Friday's hearing. She announced plans last week to name Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, to examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Justice Department had violated ethics or misled her during the course of the case. ___ Associated Press writer Eric Tucker contributed to this report. item.title: A botched router upgrade grounded flights nationwide. Now questions are mounting.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By David Shepardson WASHINGTON, Nov 14 (Reuters) - US air travel is not expected to return to normal schedules until late on Sunday, the head of the FAA said, as the aviation system gradually recovers from a nationwide flight shutdown that officials blamed on routine maintenance gone awry. As of 9:35 p.m. ET (0235 GMT), airlines on Saturday had ‌canceled more than 6,400 US flights and delayed more than 8,000, according to FlightAware, an aviation website. That followed about 9,200 flights canceled and 7,500 delayed on Friday after ‌the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop because of disruptions to air traffic communications. FlightAware said 875 flights scheduled for Sunday were already canceled. Federal Aviation Administration head Bryan Bedford said on Saturday that he expected airline operations to largely return to ​normal by late Sunday. He also apologized for the disruption, adding that the system remains stable. The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday that halted nearly all departing flights for almost five hours. It was the longest nationwide halt to air travel since the attacks of September 11, 2001, and one of the single worst US travel days ever. The issue prompted the White House to convene an emergency meeting in the Situation Room on Friday and federal agencies to scramble to determine if it was a cyberattack. But the problem was traced to FAA contractor L3Harris' installation of at least one new router at a remote ‌facility, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Saturday. "We're working to determine ⁠whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router? We haven't determined what the fault was," Duffy said at a press conference. The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists, a union representing FAA safety employees, said the issue was isolated to two ⁠routers that were updated Friday. An official told Reuters it was believed the routers were in Arkansas and Texas. An FAA official said the agency conducted a safety assessment before the work. The union said PASS-represented technicians were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop. L3Harris said it took the issue seriously and is supporting the FAA in its investigation. Its shares last traded down about 4% after hours on ​Friday. OVERLOADED ​COMMUNICATIONS CENTERS Duffy said the trouble began on Friday afternoon, when air traffic control centers experienced instability in radar ​and communications systems. The router issue led to data overloading other communications centers, ‌officials said. "We had over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, and what that did was (it) gave us issues with our communication with airplanes, and it also caused some disruption with our radar," Duffy added. The issue affected communications at 17 of the FAA's 22 en route centers, which control aircraft during the cruise portion of a flight. Bedford said the FAA ordered the ground stop in case a center lost all communications. "No facilities went dark. Nothing was fully lost," Bedford added. The FAA said it was doing additional testing with L3Harris to see if there are any additional risks. Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and American Airlines all canceled about 25% of their flights on Saturday, while JetBlue canceled nearly 45%. Airlines have issued travel waivers allowing passengers to rebook flights for later dates ‌without cost. Though the FAA lifted the ground stop on Friday evening, the disruption for passengers was far from over, with ​tens of thousands of people stranded in airports. Airlines were trying to get flight crews and other personnel in ​position to resume flights. The disruption stranded some college football teams on Friday before games ​scheduled for Saturday. FUNDS SOUGHT TO FIX SYSTEM STRAIN Friday's disruption is the latest and most dramatic sign of strain on a US air traffic control system beset ‌by aging technology, equipment and communications problems and a shortage of several ​thousand controllers. Duffy called on Friday for $50 billion in funding ​to upgrade air traffic control systems, up from his earlier request of $30 billion — after Congress approved $12.5 billion last year. House Speaker Mike Johnson told Fox News on Saturday that he supports approving more funding for air traffic this year. Johnson's Republicans control Congress until next year, when Democrats will take over because of their gains in the November 3 midterm ​elections. US Representatives Rick Larsen and Andre Carson, Democrats slated next year ‌to chair the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and aviation subcommittee, respectively, said in a joint statement Saturday that their panels will "hold the administration accountable for what happened ​to make sure this chaos does not happen again." Since receiving $12.5 billion last year, the Transportation Department has awarded contracts worth $4.3 billion but only spent $1 billion, Larsen and ​Carson said. (Reporting by David Shepardson in Washington; Editing by Nick Zieminski, Rod Nickel and Jamie Freed) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://uk.finance.yahoo.com/news/thousands-us-flights-canceled-delayed-155615998.html
